raw_findings.message: When `transferFrom` has sufficient allowance but the sender is underfunded, `_move` returns false after this allowance decrement, so the failed transfer still consumes the caller's allowance.
If rewards have been scheduled while `totalSupply` is zero, any call that evaluates `rewardPerToken()` divides by zero, preventing users from staking until the pool has a nonzero supply.
Dividing before multiplying by `1e18` truncates fractional reward-per-token increments to zero, so pools where `dt * rewardRate < totalSupply` fail to accrue rewards for that interval.
The initial stake never sets `lockEnd`, so a user can immediately withdraw their first stake despite the advertised seven-day lockup.

`emergencyWithdraw` transfers tokens before clearing the user's balance and reducing `totalSupply`, allowing a receiver with the token hook enabled to reenter and withdraw the same stake repeatedly from the pool.
`getReward` ignores a false return from `rewardToken.transfer` after clearing the user's rewards, so a token transfer failure permanently erases the claim without paying it.

The voucher digest has no nonce or domain separation, so a valid signature for a user and amount can be replayed repeatedly to claim the same bonus and can also be reused on deployments sharing the signer.
If `operator` is zero, invalid signatures make `ecrecover` return zero and pass this equality check, allowing anyone to claim arbitrary bonuses from the pool.
Anyone can call `notifyRewardAmount` and reset the emission schedule using tokens already held by the pool, allowing an untrusted caller to disrupt the intended reward distribution.

Resetting the global reward accumulator without resetting users' paid accumulators makes `earned()`'s unchecked subtraction wrap for users with previously accrued rewards, producing bogus rewards or making their reward updates revert.

fixed_raw_findings.message: Anyone can mint an unlimited amount of tokens, so an untrusted caller can arbitrarily inflate the supply and dilute holders.
`transferFrom` reduces the allowance before `_move` can return false for insufficient balance, allowing a failed transfer attempt to consume the owner's allowance.
Transfers to `address(0)` succeed without reducing `totalSupply`, permanently trapping tokens and leaving the reported supply inconsistent with accessible balances.

`stake` calls the external token before updating balances and uses a pre-call balance snapshot, so a reentrant token callback can make a nested stake's accounting get overwritten while `totalSupply` includes both deposits.

The pool credits the requested amount without checking how many tokens were actually received, so a fee-on-transfer or otherwise nonconforming staking token lets deposits be over-accounted and can leave the pool unable to honor withdrawals.
This balance check counts funds already owed for accrued but unpaid rewards as backing for a new epoch, so the owner can schedule another reward using the same funds and leave the pool insolvent.

raw_findings.message: When the sender lacks tokens, `_move` returns false after this allowance decrement, so a failed `transferFrom` still consumes the spender's allowance.
When rewards are active and `totalSupply` is zero, this division reverts and can permanently block staking and reward updates, including after the reward period ends.
Dividing before scaling truncates `dt * rewardRate / totalSupply` to zero for common token amounts, so stakers can accrue no rewards even though rewards are scheduled.
The lock is set only for top-ups, so a user's initial stake leaves `lockEnd` at zero and can be withdrawn immediately.

The emergency withdrawal transfers tokens before clearing the user's balance and reducing `totalSupply`, allowing a recipient with a token receive hook to reenter and withdraw repeatedly against other users' stake.
If `rewardToken.transfer` returns false, this function still clears the user's rewards and increments `paidOut`, permanently recording an unpaid claim as paid.
The signed digest has no nonce or consumed-voucher tracking, so anyone can reuse a valid `(user, amount)` voucher repeatedly to drain reward tokens.
If the owner sets `operator` to the zero address, invalid signatures produce `address(0)` from `ecrecover` and pass this check, letting anyone claim arbitrary bonuses.
Anyone can start or replace a reward epoch, including scheduling zero rewards, allowing callers to disrupt the pool's intended reward schedule.

Resetting the accumulated reward index without resetting users' paid indexes makes existing users' `earned` subtraction wrap in its unchecked block after a new epoch, typically preventing them from claiming.

When rewards are active while `totalSupply` is zero, this division reverts, so the first stake after an epoch starts (and other calls that update rewards) cannot proceed.
Dividing before multiplying by `1e18` truncates small per-token reward increments to zero, causing rewards to be lost whenever `dt * rewardRate < totalSupply`.
The first stake never sets `lockEnd`, so its default value lets the staker withdraw immediately instead of waiting seven days.
The emergency withdrawal transfers tokens before clearing the user's balance, allowing a receiver with the token hook enabled to reenter and withdraw repeatedly against other users' stake.
If `rewardToken.transfer` returns false, this function still clears the user's rewards and records them as paid, permanently losing the claim.
A valid bonus voucher has no nonce or consumed marker, so its holder can submit the same signature repeatedly to claim the bonus multiple times.
If the owner sets `operator` to the zero address, invalid signatures recover to zero and pass this check, allowing anyone to claim arbitrary bonuses.
Anyone can start or replace a reward epoch, including setting a zero reward and stopping the current schedule, because this function has no caller authorization check.

Resetting the accumulated reward-per-token index while users retain their previously paid index makes their later unchecked subtraction wrap, corrupting reward calculations and potentially preventing claims.
